newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Easdaq launches, but no trade likely until October.
newsitem.headline: Easdaq launches, but no trade likely until October.

text.p: Blank screens greeted dealers on Easdaq, Europe's newest equity market, on Monday as a legal hurdle stood in the way of trade on the opening day.
But Easdaq's backers remained confident this would not prevent the market in small company stocks from becoming a success.

"Obviously we would have loved to have companies trading on the first day but the key thing is all the systems are working," Easdaq spokesman Chris Pickles told Reuters. "We should have 15 companies by Christmas, which puts us well on target for meeting the goal of 50 companies by the end of the first year."

Easdaq is a Brussels-based, pan-European, screen-based market for growth stocks modelled on the United States' Nasdaq exchange. It targets European companies already listed on Nasdaq as well as new issues.

Companies seeking admission are Belgian bio-tech firm Innogenetics, Belgian software firm Artwork Systems, German software firm Creatix, U.S. clinical testing firm UniHolding Corp and U.K. vehicle management firm Pride Automotive Group. The last two have Nasdaq listings.
Canada's Nasdaq-listed bio-tech firm DynaMotive Technologies also plans to seek an Easdaq listing.
However, the rules governing admissions were not approved by Belgium's finance ministry until last Thursday, leaving companies just one day to formally apply for a listing.
Applications for listings must legally be approved by Easdaq and Belgium's regulatory Banking and Finance Commission before quotation in any issue can begin.
"We expect to have several shares quoted before the end of (October)," said a trader at KB Securities in Brussels, one of many firms vying to become Easdaq brokers.
Each company listed on Easdaq must be supported by two market makers.
Pickles said it was likely the first issue on Easdaq would be a Nasdaq-quoted European company seeking a dual listing rather than a company issuing new capital.
Initial public offerings (IPOs) would follow later. "We would never have recommended them on day one," he said.
Despite the procedural delay in approving Easdaq's rules, no companies waiting in the pipeline had cancelled their plans, he said.
